The reader is referred to Caunter on the Poetry of the Pentateuch, for further information respecting the poetical character of these verses; and to Bishop Newton’s Dissertations, No. I., for its prophetical application. Some excellent remarks, of a practical kind, will be found in Bishop Hall’s contemplations. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1368" type="x-p"/> </note> It is asked in the first place, why Noah instead of pronouncing the curse upon his son, inflicts the severity of punishment, which that son had deserved, upon his innocent grandson; since it seems not consistent with the justice of God, to visit the crimes of parents upon their children? But the answer is well known; namely that God, although he pursues his course of judgments upon the sons and the grandchildren of the ungodly, yet in being angry with them, is not angry with the innocent, because even they themselves are found in fault. Wherefore there is no absurdity in the act of avenging the sins of the fathers upon their reprobate children; since, of necessity, all those whom God has deprived of his Spirit are subject to his wrath. But it is surprising that Noah should curse his grandson; and should pass his son Ham, the author of the crime, over in silence. The Jews imagine that the reason of this was to be traced to the special favor of God; and that since the Lord had bestowed on Ham so great an honor, <note n="299"> <div sID="gen1369" type="x-p"/> Namely, that of having preserved him in the ark. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1369" type="x-p"/> </note> the curse was transferred from him to his son. But the conjecture is futile. Certainly, to my mind, there is no doubt that the punishment was carried forward even to his posterity in order that the severity of it might be the more apparent; as if the Lord had openly proclaimed that the punishment of one man would not satisfy him but that he would attach the curse also to the posterity of the offender, so that it should extend through successive ages. In the meantime, Ham himself is so far from being exempt, that God, by involving his son with him, aggravates his own condemnation.<div eID="gen1361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1370" type="x-p"/>Another question is also proposed; namely, why among the many sons of Ham, God chooses one to be smitten? But let not our curiosity here indulge itself too freely; let us remember that the judgments of God are, not in vain, called “a great deep,” and that it would be a degrading thing for God, before whose tribunal we all must one day stand, to be subjected to our judgments, or rather to our foolish temerity. He chooses whom he sees good, that he may show forth in them an example of his grace and kindness; others he appoints to a different end, that they may be proofs of his anger and severity. Here, although the minds of men are blinded, let every one of us, conscious of his own infirmity, learn rather to ascribe praise to God’s justice, than plunge, with insane audacity, into the profound abyss. While God held the whole seed of Ham as obnoxious to the curse, he mentions the Canaanites by name, as those whom he would curse above all others. And hence we infer that this judgment proceeded from God, because it was proved by the event itself. What would certainly be the condition of the Canaanites, Noah could not know by human means. Wherefore in things obscure and hidden, the Spirit directed his tongue.<div eID="gen1370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1371" type="x-p"/>Another difficulty still remains: for since the Scripture teaches that God avenges the sins of men on the third and fourth generation, it seems to assign this limit to the wrath of God; but the vengeance of which mention is now made extends itself to the tenth generation. I answer, that these words of Scripture are not intended to prescribe a law to God, which he may not so far set aside, as to be at liberty to punish sins beyond four generations. The thing to be here observed is, the comparison instituted between punishment and grace; by which we are taught, that God, while he is a just avenger of crimes, is still more inclined to mercy. In the meantime, let his liberty remain unquestioned, to extend his vengeance as far as he pleases.<div eID="gen1371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1372" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">A</hi> <hi type="italic">servant</hi> <hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">servants</hi> <hi type="italic">shall</hi> <hi type="italic">he</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> . This Hebraism signifies that Canaan shall be the last, even among servants: as if it had been said, ‘Not only shall his condition be servile, but worse than that of common servitude.’ <note n="300"> <div sID="gen1373" type="x-p"/> Vide Ainsworth in loco, Bishop Newton’s Dissertation i.<div eID="gen1373" type="x-p"/> </note> Yet the thunder of this severe and dreadful prophecy seems weak and illusory, since the Canaanites excelled in strength and in riches, and were possessed of extensive dominion. Where then is this servitude? In the first place, I answer, that though God, in threatening men, does not immediately execute what he denounces, yet his threats are never weak and ineffectual. Secondly, that the judgments of God are not always exhibited before our eyes, nor apprehended by our carnal reason. The Canaanites, having shaken off the yoke of servitude, which was divinely imposed upon them, even proceeded to grasp at empire for themselves. But although they triumph for a time, yet in the sight of God their condition is not deemed free. Just as when the faithful are iniquitously oppressed, and tyrannically harassed by the wicked, their spiritual liberty is still not extinct in the sight of God. It behaves us then to be content with this proof of the divine judgment, that God promised the dominion of the land of Canaan to his servant Abraham, and at length devoted the Canaanites to destruction. But because the Pope so earnestly maintains that he sometimes utters prophecies, — as did even Caiaphas, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.11.51">John 11:51</reference>,) — lest we should seem to refuse him everything, I do not deny that the title with which he adorns himself was dictated by the Spirit of God, ‘Let him be a servant of servants,’ in the same sense that Canaan was.<div eID="gen1372" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.9.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen1360" osisID="Gen.9.25" type="section"/>
entries.e798b83e3bbdc315b69c2c37282ffaa8cf34207f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.9.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.9.26" sID="gen1374" type="section"/> <div sID="gen1375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">Blessed</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">God</hi> <hi type="italic">of</hi> <hi type="italic">Shem</hi> . Noah blesses his other children, but in a different manner. For he places Shem in the highest post of honor. And this is the reason why Noah, in blessing him, breaks forth in the praise of God, without adhering to the person of man. For the Hebrews, when they are speaking of any rare and transcendent excellence, raise their thoughts to God. Therefore the holy man, when he perceived that the most abundant grace of God was destined for his son Shem, rises to thanksgiving. Whence we infer, that he spoke, not from carnal reason, but rather treated of the secret favors of God, the result of which was to be deferred to a remote period. Finally, by these words it is declared, that the benediction of Shem would be divine or heavenly.<div eID="gen1375" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.9.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen1374" osisID="Gen.9.26" type="section"/>
entries.b93dc97fb6d21b9e755725015e07b1c8602a9056: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.9.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.9.27" sID="gen1376" type="section"/> <div sID="gen1377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> <hi type="italic">God</hi> <hi type="italic">shall</hi> <hi type="italic">enlarge</hi> <hi type="italic">Japheth</hi> . In the Hebrew words <foreign xml:lang="he">יפת</foreign> ( <hi type="italic">japhte</hi> ) and <foreign xml:lang="he">יפת</foreign> ( <hi type="italic">japheth</hi> ,) there is an elegant allusion. For the root of the word is <foreign xml:lang="he">פתה</foreign> ( <hi type="italic">pathah</hi> ,) which, among the Hebrews, signifies to entice with smooth words, or to allure in one direction or another. Here, however, nearly all commentators take it as signifying to enlarge. <note n="301"> <div sID="gen1378" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="la">Dilatet Deus Japheth</foreign>.” — <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi> . “<foreign xml:lang="el">πλατύναι ὅ Θεὸς</foreign>” — <hi type="italic">Sept</hi><div eID="gen1378" type="x-p"/> </note> If this exposition be received, the meaning will be, that the posterity of Japheth, which for a time would be scattered, and removed far from the tents of Shem, would at length be increased, so that it should more nearly approach them, and should dwell together with them, as in a common home. But I rather approve the other version, ‘God shall gently bring back, or incline Japheth.’ <note n="302"> <div sID="gen1379" type="x-p"/> See marginal reading of English version, “God will persuade Japheth.” — See also Schindler’s Lexicon, sub voce <foreign xml:lang="he">פתה</foreign>, and Ainsworth in loco. It is however objected, and not without reason, that the word here rendered <hi type="italic">persuade</hi> is rarely, if ever, used in a good sense, that it generally means to entice, or allure to evil; and, therefore, the most judicious critics seem rather inclined to fall back upon the version given in the text of our translation, than to accept the marginal reading, with which Calvin agrees. See Professor Bush’s note on this place. Dathe gives the preference to the Arabic version, which signifies that God will prosper Japheth; but for this there is no sufficient authority. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen1379" type="x-p"/> </note> Moreover, whichever interpretation we follow, Noah predicts that there will be a temporary dissension between Shem and Japheth, although he retains both in his family and calls both his lawful heirs; and that afterwards the time will come, in which they shall again coalesce in one body, and have a common home. It is, however, most absolutely certain, that a prophecy is here put forth concerning things unknown to man, of which, as the event, at length, shows God alone was the Author. Two thousand years and some centuries more, elapsed before the Gentiles and the Jews were gathered together in one faith. Then the sons of Shem, of whom the greater part had revolted and cut themselves off from the holy family of God, were collected together, and dwelt under one tabernacle. <note n="303"> <div sID="gen1380" type="x-p"/> Allusion here seems to be made to the words quoted by James from the prophecy of Amos: “I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; and I will build again the ruins thereof and I will set it up.” — <reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.16">Acts 15:16</reference>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1380" type="x-p"/> </note> Also the Gentiles, the progeny of Japheth, who had long been wanderers and fugitives were received into the same tabernacle. For God, by a new adoption, has formed a people out of those who were separated, and has confirmed a fraternal union between alienated parties. This is done by the sweet and gentle voice of God, which he has uttered in the gospel; and this prophecy is still daily receiving its fulfillment, since God invites the scattered sheep to join his flock, and collects, on every side, those who shall sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven. It is truly no common support of our faith, that the calling of the Gentiles is not only decreed in the eternal counsel of God, but is openly declared by the mouth of the Patriarch; lest we should think it to have happened suddenly or by chance, that the inheritance of eternal life was offered generally to all. But the form of the expression, ‘Japheth shall dwell in the tabernacles of Shem,’ <note n="304"> <div sID="gen1381" type="x-p"/> It is not clear whether the original really means that “Japheth,” or that “God,” “shall dwell in the tents of Shem.” If the former, then this is a plain prediction of events which have been in a remarkable manner fulfilled, by the conversion of the Gentiles, and by the diffusion of a vast European population over those regions which were originally occupied by the descendants of Shem. If the original really means the latter, then it has been fulfilled by the manifestation of God’s glory among the Israelites, first through the Shechinah which appeared in the tabernacle and temple, and then more especially through the advent of the Messiah, of whom St. John says, “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us; and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.14">John 1:14</reference>.) — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen1381" type="x-p"/> </note> commends to us that mutual society which ought to exist, and to be cherished among the faithful. For whereas God had chosen to himself a Church from the progeny of Shem, he afterwards chose the Gentiles together with them, on this condition, that they should join themselves to that people, who were in possession of the covenant of life.<div eID="gen1377" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.9.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen1376" osisID="Gen.9.27" type="section"/>

28. And Noah lived . Although Moses briefly states the age of the holy man, and does not record his annals and the memorable events of his life, yet those things which are certain, and which Scripture elsewhere commemorates, ought to recur to our minds. Within one hundred and fifty years, the offspring of his three sons became so numerous, that he had sufficient and even abundant proof of the efficacy of the Divine benediction Increase and multiply. He sees, not one city only, filled with his grandchildren, nor his seed expanded barely to three hundred families; but many nations springing from one of his sons who should inhabit extensive regions. This astonishing increase, since it was a visible representation of the divine favor towards him, would doubtless fill him with unbounded joy. For Abraham was nearly fifty years old when his ancestor Noah died.
Lightfoot places the death of Noah two years before the birth of Abraham; Dr. A. Clarke two years after it. These chronological differences, however, do not materially affect the general conclusions drawn by Calvin. — Ed.
In the meantime, he was compelled to behold many things, which would afflict his holy breast with incredible grief. To omit other things; he saw in the family of Shem, the sanctuary of God, — into which the sons of Japheth were to be received, — destroyed, or, at least, dilapidated and rent. For whereas the father of Abraham himself, having deserted his proper station, had erected for himself a profane tabernacle; a very small portion indeed remained of those who worshipped God in the harmonious consent of a pure faith. With what tormenting pains this terrible confusion affected him cannot be sufficiently expressed in words. Hence we may know, that his eyes of faith must have been exceedingly penetrating, which did not fail to behold afar of, the grace of God, in preserving the Church, at that time overwhelmed by the wickedness of men.

                  <ns0:p n="15">15. And I will remember my Covenant which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> between me and you, and every <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> every living Soul in all flesh.</ns0:note> living Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture of all Flesh: and the Waters shall no more become a Flood to destroy all Flesh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. And the Bow shall be in the Cloud, and I will look upon it, that I may remember the Ever<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lasting Covenant <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> This Covenant made with all succeeding Generations of men and Beasts. This and the like speeches are oft ascri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bed to God after the manner of Men, who being forgetfull need helps for their memory.</ns0:note>, between God and every liv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Creature of all Flesh that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon the Earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. And God said unto <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken of the Covenant <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The same thing is so oft repeated for the strengthning of the Faith of all men, and especially of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> and his Sons, whom the remembrance of that dreadful deluge, which they had experience of, had made exceeding prone to fears of the like for time to come.</ns0:note> which I have established be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween me and all Flesh, that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon the Earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. And the Sons of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> that went forth of the Ark, were <ns0:hi>Shem,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ham,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iapheth:</ns0:hi> And <ns0:hi>Ham is</ns0:hi> the Father of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Chanaan.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which is here mentioned to make way for the follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing relation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. These <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the three Sons of <ns0:hi>Noah:</ns0:hi> And of them was the whole Earth overspread <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">A Truth which the old Heathens were not ignorant of, though they changed the Names, and mixed their Fables with it, for they tell us that <ns0:hi>Saturn,</ns0:hi> and his three Sons divid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the World among themselves. And it is apparent that their Saturn was no other than our <ns0:hi>Noah,</ns0:hi> because they tell us he was the common Parent and Prince of all mankind, also an Husbandman and Vine-dresser, all which <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> was: They say he was born of the Sea, because <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> came out of the Waters: That he devoured all his Children except three, because <ns0:hi>Noah condemned</ns0:hi> and foretold the destruction of all the rest of <ns0:hi>the World.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. And <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> began <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> an Husbandman <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Was an Husbandman, as he had been before. The Verb, <ns0:hi>to begin,</ns0:hi> doth oft abound, and is applied to him that continueth or repeateth an action begun before. Thus Christ is said to <ns0:hi>begin to cast out, Mark</ns0:hi> 11. 15. and to <ns0:hi>begin to speak, Luk.</ns0:hi> 12. 1. For which in the parallel places he is said only <ns0:hi>to cast out, Matth.</ns0:hi> 21. 12. and <ns0:hi>to speak<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Matth.</ns0:hi> 16. 6.</ns0:note>, and he planted a Vineyard.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. And he drank of the Wine, and was drun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either through ignorance and inexperience of the nature and strength of that Liquor, or through the infirmity of the Flesh, which was tempted by its great and to him new plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />santness, and by the refreshment he found in it, under the weary labours of his Body, and the sad thoughts of his mind for the desolate condition of the World.</ns0:note>, and he was uncovered <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either to releive him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self against the heat of the Climate and Season, or from his negligence and carelessness, which might easily happen, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause mens garments at that time were loose, as they were in the following ages, when breeches were not in common use, and therefore were peculiarly prescribed to the Priests, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 28. 42. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 44. 18, 19.</ns0:note> within his Tent.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. And <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whose grown age was a great aggravation of this sin.</ns0:note>, the Father of <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This is here added as a reason of <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi>'s Curse. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 25.</ns0:note> saw the nakedness <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> The secret parts, oft so called, as <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 18. and else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where.</ns0:note> of his Father, and told his two Brethren without <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Who were then without the house or room where their Father lay in that posture, whom he invited to that prospect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. And <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iapheth</ns0:hi> took a Garment, and laid <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> upon both their shoulders, and went backward, and covered the nakedness of their Father, and their faces <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> backward, and they saw not their Fathers nakedness.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. And <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> awoke from his Wine <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> From his drunkenness, or from his sleep, the ef<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fect of it.</ns0:note>, and knew <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either by the information of his Sons: Or by di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine inspiration.</ns0:note> what his younger Son <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>His little Son,</ns0:hi> either <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 22. or <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> mentioned in the next verse; by comparing of which places it may be gathered, that <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> first saw it, and told his Father <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> of it, and he told it to his Brethren. The latter seems here principally intended, 1. Because the curse following is appropriated to him. 2. Because of the title of <ns0:hi>younger</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>little Son,</ns0:hi> which seems not to be so pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly added if <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> was meant, both because it doth not appear that he was the youngest, for wheresoever these three Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren are mentioned, he is always put in the middle place, and because that addition seems to be unnecessary and imper<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinent to the present business, which if <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> be intended, is proper and pertinent by way of distinction, to shew that he spake of his Grandson, o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> his Sons Son. <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> He calleth him his <ns0:hi>Son. Answ.</ns0:hi> Grand-children are frequently called their Grand-fathers Sons in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 29. 5. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 24. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 1. 17.</ns0:note> had done unto him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. And he said <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not from the passion of revenge, but by divine inspiration, and the Spirit of Prophesie.</ns0:note>, Cursed <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Hateful to God, ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />horred by men, miserable in his person and posterity.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>be Canaan</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> Seeing <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> committed the crime, why is the curse inflicted up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on his Son <ns0:hi>Canaan? Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. When <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> is not exempted from the curse, but rather more deeply plunged into it, whilest he is pronounced accursed, not only in his person (which is manifestly supposed by his commission of that sin for which the curse was inflicted) but also in his posterity, which doubtless was a great aggravation of his grief: As on the contrary <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> is said to be blessed, when his Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren are blessed, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 48. 15, 16. 2. It seems therefore very pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable from these words, and the Hebrew Doctors and others affirm it, that <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> did partake with his Father in the sin, yea that he was the first discoverer of his Fathers shame. 3. <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> is particularly mentioned by the spirit of Prophes<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e, in regard of the future extirpation of that people, and this is here remembred for the encouragement of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> who were now in their expedition against them. 4. This may be an ellipsis or defect of the word, <ns0:hi>Father;</ns0:hi> for such relative words are oft-times omitted and understood in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 4. 21. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Zebedee,</ns0:hi> for, <ns0:hi>the Son of Zebedee. Ioh.</ns0:hi> 19. 25. <ns0:hi>Mary of Cl<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>opas,</ns0:hi> for, <ns0:hi>the wife of Cleopas. Act.</ns0:hi> 7. 16. <ns0:hi>Emmor of Sychem,</ns0:hi> for, <ns0:hi>the Father of Sychem,</ns0:hi> as our English Translation rightly supplies it from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 33. 19. Thus <ns0:hi>Goliah</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>Goliahs Brother,</ns0:hi> as is evident by comparing 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 19. with 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20, 5. So here <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> may be put for, <ns0:hi>the Father of Canaan,</ns0:hi> as the Arabick Translation hath it, that is, <ns0:hi>Ham,</ns0:hi> as the <ns0:hi>seventy</ns0:hi> here render it. And though <ns0:hi>Ham</ns0:hi> had more Sons, yet he may be here described by his relation to <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> because in him the Curse was more fixed and dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, reaching to his utter extirpation, whilst the rest of <ns0:hi>Hams</ns0:hi> posterity in after ages were blessed with the saving knowledge of the Gospel.</ns0:note>, a Ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant of Servants <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> The vilest and worst of Servants; as <ns0:hi>vanity of vanities,</ns0:hi> is the greatest vanity, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 1. 2. and <ns0:hi>great wickedness, Hos.</ns0:hi> 10. 15. is in the Hebrew <ns0:hi>wickedness of wickedness,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>King of Kings</ns0:hi> is put for the chief of Kings.</ns0:note> shall he be unto his Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. And he said, Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the Lord God of <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> What is this to <ns0:hi>Sem?</ns0:hi> For it is not <ns0:hi>Sem,</ns0:hi> but God, who is here blessed. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> also is here blessed, and that in the highest degree, because the Lord hath here declared himself to be <ns0:hi>Shems</ns0:hi> God. Now for God to be said to be any mans God is every where mentioned as the height of blessed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17. 7. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 144. 15. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 31. 33. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 22. 32. But the phrase is here justly varied. The curse is fixed upon <ns0:hi>Ham,</ns0:hi> because man alone is the Author of his own sin, and the cause of his ruine: But because God is the Author and Fountain of all the good that man either doth or receiv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth, therefore the blessing is emphatically given to God; who only doth the work and of right is to receive all the glory, yet so as it redounds to <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> also. And <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> is here pecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liarly mentioned, not <ns0:hi>Iapheth,</ns0:hi> both for the comfort of the <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raelites,</ns0:hi> whose Progenitor he was, and because this blessing was first seated and long continued in <ns0:hi>Shems</ns0:hi> Posterity alone, <ns0:hi>Iapheths</ns0:hi> Posterity being for a long time excluded from it, and because the Lord Christ, who is often called <ns0:hi>the Lord</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> in Scripture did take Flesh from <ns0:hi>Shem,</ns0:hi> and so the In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />carnation of Christ may be here foretold, and <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> highly honoured and blessed in this, that he should be the Father of Christ according to the Flesh, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9. 5. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 2. This may be a short and abrupt manner of speech, which is frequent in the Hebrew Tongue, and it may signifie that <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> should be so eminently blessed, that men beholding it should be wrapt up into admiration, and break forth into the praises of that God who gave such gifts unto men and did so great things for <ns0:hi>S<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>m. Answ.</ns0:hi> 3. The words may be otherwise rendred, either thus <ns0:hi>b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>essed<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> O Lord God,</ns0:hi> let <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> be, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Do thou bless him: So it is only the construct form, <ns0:hi>Elohe,</ns0:hi> for the absolute <ns0:hi>Elohim,</ns0:hi> which is not unusual in Scripture: or thus, <ns0:hi>Blessed</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>the Lord God</ns0:hi> be <ns0:hi>Shem,</ns0:hi> or shall <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> be. So here is only a defect of the Hebrew parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cle <ns0:hi>min,</ns0:hi> which is oft wanting.</ns0:note>; and <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> shall be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Servant to them.</ns0:note> his Servant.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:13" />27. God shall <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> perswade.</ns0:note> enlarge <ns0:hi>Iapheth</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Enlarge to Iapheth,</ns0:hi> understand here <ns0:hi>his place,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 22. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 4. 1. or <ns0:hi>his border:</ns0:hi> Which was very literally made good to him, because he had a very numerous Poste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity, and by them he possessed the largest part of the World, even all <ns0:hi>Europe,</ns0:hi> a great part of <ns0:hi>Asia,</ns0:hi> and as it is probable <ns0:hi>America</ns0:hi> also. Or, <ns0:hi>God shall perswade Iapheth,</ns0:hi> to do what fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows, to dwell in <ns0:hi>Shems</ns0:hi> Tents, where God dwelleth, and so to be re-united to his Brother <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> both in affection and in Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligion, in both which the Gentiles, the greatest part of whom were <ns0:hi>Iapheths</ns0:hi> Posterity, were for a long time at an irreconcile<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able distance from the Jews.</ns0:note>, and he shall dwell in the Tents of <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>(i. e.)</ns0:hi> Shall be of the same Church with <ns0:hi>Shem, i. e.</ns0:hi> of the Church, which is called in Scripture <ns0:hi>the Tents</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Tabernacles of Iudah,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>of Iacob,</ns0:hi> or in general, <ns0:hi>of the Saints, Zach.</ns0:hi> 12. 7. <ns0:hi>Mal</ns0:hi> 2. 12. <ns0:hi>Revel.</ns0:hi> 20. 9. and here, <ns0:hi>of Shem</ns0:hi> in whose Posterity the Church was first and longest settled. And <ns0:hi>to dwell</ns0:hi> with another, notes friendly as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sociation and communion with him, as when God is said to <ns0:hi>dwell with men:</ns0:hi> And when <ns0:hi>the Wolf</ns0:hi> is said to <ns0:hi>dwell with the Lamb, Isa.</ns0:hi> 11. 6. Possibly this may note <ns0:hi>Iapheths</ns0:hi> Succession into <ns0:hi>Shems</ns0:hi> Tents, or coming into their place and stead, or the calling of the Gentiles together with the rejection of Jews: as the <ns0:hi>Reubenites</ns0:hi> are said to <ns0:hi>dwell in the Tabernacles of the Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />garens</ns0:hi> whom they subdued and expelled, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron</ns0:hi> 5. 10.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi> shall be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> servant to them.</ns0:note> his Servant <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This was eminently accomplished: For though <ns0:hi>Shem</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iapheth</ns0:hi> in their Posterity did successively conquer and rule one over the other, yet none of <ns0:hi>Hams</ns0:hi> Posterity did ever bear rule over <ns0:hi>Iapheth,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Ham,</ns0:hi> though for a time he bore sway in his Son <ns0:hi>Nimrod,</ns0:hi> yet that dominion soon expired, and the <ns0:hi>Assrrians, Chaldeans, Grecians,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> ruled the World for a succession of many Ages; and <ns0:hi>Hams</ns0:hi> people were constantly their Servants and Subjects.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. And <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> lived after the Flood three hundred and fifty years <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which reacheth to the fifty eighth year of <ns0:hi>Abrahams</ns0:hi> Age, as the Jews note. And so we have a manifest account of the propagation of Religion from the beginning of the World to this day. <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> received it from his Parents, who had the ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count of it from their first Father <ns0:hi>Adams</ns0:hi> own mouth, and transmitted it to <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and its descent from him to the Jews, and by the Jews to others is sufficiently known<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Within this time also <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> saw the Building of <ns0:hi>Babels</ns0:hi> Tower, the horrid Wickedness and Idolatry of his Children, and the bloody Wars which even then arose between some of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29. And all the days of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> were nine hundred and fifty years <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Here is an omission of that solemn clause used in all the preceding Generations, <ns0:hi>and he begat Sons and Daughters,</ns0:hi> which implies that <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> had no more than these three Sons, which also appears from the 19th. verse of this Chapter.</ns0:note>, and he died.</ns0:p>
